We need to deduce second analytical group cations (acid-insoluble sulfide). Typically group includes cations that form sulfide precipitates insoluble in acid: e.g., Pb2+, Bi3+, Cu2+, Cd2+, Hg2+, Ag+, etc? Actually classification: In qualitative analysis, second group (acid-insoluble sulfides) includes cations that form black precipitates with H2S in acidic medium: Pb2+, Bi3+, Cu2+, Cd2+, Hg2+, Ag+. Also maybe As3+, Sb3+? But typical scheme: Group II: Pb2+, Bi3+, Cu2+, Cd2+, Hg2+, Ag+. They form sulfides insoluble in dilute HCl. So we need to test for these.

We already have Hg2+2 identified from first group (insoluble chloride). Mercury(I) chloride is insoluble, so Hg2+ is already present. It also belongs to second group? Mercury(I) sulfide is also insoluble. So second group may include Hg2+ as well, but we already know it's present. The question: "Identifying cations from the second analytical group (acid-insoluble sulfide)." So we need to list which of those cations are present in the sample. Since we already have Hg2+, we need to see if any other group II cations present.

We have performed tests: adding HCl 1M to sample gave precipitate (white). That could be Hg2Cl2 (white). Then adding NH3 gave blue supernatant, precipitate still white. That suggests dissolution of some precipitate? Actually Hg2Cl2 is insoluble in NH3? It forms [Hg(NH3)2]Cl? Not sure. But the blue supernatant suggests formation of Cu(OH)2?
